subject: Environment
sub_topic: CPCB and SPCB — composition and powers

concepts.name: Statutory Basis and Parent Legislation of CPCB vs SPCB
key_dimensions: CPCB established under Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 — NOT Environment Protection Act, 1986
SPCBs also created under Water Act 1974, but Air Act 1981 extended their mandate — trap: they are NOT separate bodies under Air Act
Distinction between CPCB's role under Water Act, Air Act, and Environment Protection Act as an advisory/technical arm of MoEFCC
Why no separate board was created under EPA 1986 — CPCB and SPCBs subsumed into its framework

concepts.name: Composition of CPCB: Membership and Representation Structure
key_dimensions: CPCB has a Chairman (full-time), members representing Central Government ministries, and members representing SPCBs — exact numbers and categories under Section 3 of Water Act
UPSC trap: Chairman is appointed by Central Government, NOT elected by members
Mandatory representation of at least 5 SPCBs on CPCB — federal character of the body
Non-official members (representing interests of agriculture, fishery, industry) — often overlooked category

concepts.name: Composition of SPCBs: State-Level Structure and Variation
key_dimensions: SPCB Chairman appointed by State Government; members include representatives of local authorities, state government departments, and industries
UPSC trap: Union Territories do NOT have SPCBs — they fall under CPCB's direct jurisdiction (Section 4 of Water Act)
Mandatory inclusion of persons with knowledge of environmental science — qualitative membership criterion
Difference in composition between SPCB under Water Act and the extended role under Air Act — same body, no new composition

concepts.name: Hierarchical Relationship: CPCB's Supervisory Role over SPCBs
key_dimensions: CPCB can issue directions to SPCBs under Section 18 of Water Act — binding directions, not merely advisory
CPCB can dissolve an SPCB if it fails to perform its functions — extreme supervisory power often missed
SPCBs must submit annual reports to CPCB; CPCB consolidates and submits to Central Government
Distinction: CPCB supervises SPCBs but does NOT control them on day-to-day state matters — cooperative federalism angle

concepts.name: Powers of CPCB Under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
key_dimensions: Advisory functions to Central Government on water pollution matters (Section 16)
Power to collect and disseminate information, conduct and sponsor research on water pollution
Power to lay down standards for streams and wells — CPCB sets national standards, SPCBs may set stricter but NOT laxer standards
Power to perform functions of an SPCB in Union Territories — direct operational role

concepts.name: Powers of CPCB Under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
key_dimensions: CPCB can declare any area as an 'air pollution control area' in consultation with State Government
Power to lay down standards for emission of air pollutants from automobiles — trap: this power is with CPCB, not Ministry of Transport
CPCB approves or rejects applications for consent to operate industries in air pollution control areas at central level
Interaction with Bureau of Energy Efficiency and Motor Vehicles Act — overlapping jurisdictions

concepts.name: Consent Mechanism: 'Consent to Establish' and 'Consent to Operate'
key_dimensions: Two-stage consent under Water Act: Consent to Establish (before setting up industry) and Consent to Operate (before commencing discharge)
Consent granted by SPCB for industries in states; CPCB for UTs — jurisdictional clarity
UPSC trap: industries on the 'Red Category' list require mandatory environmental clearance AND consent — these are NOT the same thing
Deemed consent provision: if SPCB does not respond within specified period, consent is deemed granted — recent amendments

concepts.name: Power to Restrict or Prohibit Industrial Operations: Section 33A and Directions Power
key_dimensions: Section 33A of Water Act empowers boards to issue directions to close, prohibit, or regulate any industry — quasi-judicial power
These directions are enforceable; non-compliance is a criminal offence
Difference between directions under Section 33A (Water Act) and directions under Section 5 of EPA 1986 — EPA directions come from Central Government, not CPCB directly
Judicial scrutiny: Courts have upheld CPCB/SPCB shutdown orders as reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6)

concepts.name: CPCB's Role Under the Environment Protection Act, 1986: Advisory vs Executive Powers
key_dimensions: UPSC trap: CPCB does NOT have independent powers under EPA 1986 — it acts as a technical and advisory arm of MoEFCC
Central Government can delegate its EPA powers to CPCB — delegation, not inherent power
CPCB issues environmental standards (effluent standards, ambient air quality standards) notified under EPA 1986 — standard-setting role
Distinction between MoEFCC (policy), CPCB (technical/monitoring), and NGT (adjudication)

concepts.name: National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) and Effluent Standards: CPCB's Standard-Setting Role
key_dimensions: CPCB prescribes NAAQS — these are national minimum standards; states cannot lower them but can make them stricter
Industry-specific effluent standards notified under EPA 1986 on CPCB recommendations — delegated legislation angle
CPCB classifies industries into Red, Orange, Green, White categories based on Pollution Index — not a statutory classification but a regulatory tool
Recent revision of NAAQS 2009 and ongoing debate about aligning with WHO guidelines — policy controversy

concepts.name: Industrial Classification by CPCB: Red, Orange, Green, White Categories
key_dimensions: Classification based on Pollution Index (PI) score calculated from air, water, land pollution and hazardous waste parameters
Red (PI ≥ 60), Orange (41–59), Green (21–40), White (≤20) — White category industries are virtually pollution-free
UPSC trap: classification is done by CPCB but consent and monitoring is done by SPCB — division of roles
White category industries are exempt from SPCB consent requirement — significant ease-of-doing-business implication

concepts.name: Powers Related to Sampling, Inspection, and Entry: Quasi-Police Powers of Boards
key_dimensions: Boards can depute officers to enter, inspect, and take samples from any industry or water body — Section 21 and 23 of Water Act
Procedure for sample collection is prescribed — failure to follow procedure invalidates the sample as evidence (legal trap)
Power to seek assistance of police for entry and inspection when access is denied
Penalty for obstructing board officers — criminal liability under Water Act

concepts.name: Appellate Authority Against SPCB Decisions
key_dimensions: Aggrieved parties can appeal against SPCB consent refusal or conditions to the State Appellate Authority under Water Act
UPSC trap: Appeal does NOT lie to CPCB — it lies to a separate Appellate Authority constituted by State Government
Post-NGT Act 2010, many appeals now go to National Green Tribunal — overlap and jurisdictional shift
Difference between NGT jurisdiction (substantial environmental questions) and Appellate Authority (consent-related disputes)

concepts.name: National Green Tribunal vs CPCB/SPCB: Overlapping Jurisdiction and Tension
key_dimensions: NGT can suo motu take cognizance and direct CPCB/SPCB to take action — NGT is superior but not a 'supervisory' body in statutory sense
CPCB submits compliance reports to NGT — monitoring and accountability function
Tension: CPCB's own inaction has been penalized by NGT (e.g., NGT imposed costs on CPCB for failing to monitor Ganga pollution)
NGT cannot replace CPCB's technical standard-setting role — jurisdictional boundary

concepts.name: Financial Powers and Autonomy of CPCB and SPCBs
key_dimensions: CPCB funded through grants from Central Government and cess collected under Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977
UPSC trap: Cess is collected by SPCB from industries, a portion is given to CPCB — revenue-sharing mechanism
SPCBs can levy fees for consent applications — own revenue generation
Concern about SPCBs' financial dependence on state governments creating conflicts of interest — governance issue

concepts.name: Water Cess Act, 1977: Link to CPCB and SPCB Funding
key_dimensions: Cess levied on industries and local bodies consuming water for specified purposes — raises funds for pollution control
Rebate of 25% on cess if industry installs treatment plant and consumes water below prescribed norms — incentive mechanism
SPCB is the assessing and collecting authority; Central Government receives cess — SPCB acts as agent
UPSC trap: Cess under this Act is a Central levy (Entry 97, Union List), not a State levy, though SPCB collects it

concepts.name: Chairperson: Tenure, Qualifications, and Removal — Institutional Independence
key_dimensions: CPCB Chairman's qualifications: must have practical knowledge and experience in environmental matters — no strict technical degree mandated (flexibility trap)
Tenure of Chairman and members fixed; removal only through prescribed procedure — protection against arbitrary removal
UPSC trap: Chairman of CPCB is appointed by Central Government, Chairman of SPCB by State Government — parallel but separate appointment authorities
Debate on institutional independence: boards are government bodies, not independent regulators like TRAI or SEBI — policy implication

concepts.name: Inter-State Pollution Disputes: CPCB's Role as Adjudicator
key_dimensions: When pollution of a water body affects more than one state, CPCB has jurisdiction — Section 16(2)(b) of Water Act
CPCB can perform functions of an SPCB for inter-state water bodies — example: rivers crossing multiple states
UPSC trap: CPCB does not adjudicate inter-state water disputes (that is Inter-State River Water Disputes Act territory) — it addresses pollution, not water sharing
Coordination mechanism between SPCBs of different states for shared water bodies — collaborative enforcement

concepts.name: CPCB's Monitoring Networks: NAAQMS, NWMP, and Real-Time Monitoring
key_dimensions: National Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAAQMP) — CPCB operates stations across cities
National Water Quality Monitoring Programme (NWQMP) — monitors water bodies across states in collaboration with SPCBs
Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) in major cities — real-time data, feeds into AQI
UPSC angle: data generated by CPCB forms basis for policy decisions, court orders (e.g., Graded Response Action Plan in Delhi), and international reporting under conventions

concepts.name: Penalties and Prosecution Powers Under Water and Air Acts
key_dimensions: Offences under Water Act: imprisonment up to 3 months (first offence) extendable to 6 years for continuing offence — progressive penalty
UPSC trap: Boards themselves CANNOT prosecute — they must file a complaint; prosecution requires sanction from the board (Section 49 of Water Act)
Cognizance of offences only on a complaint by the Board or a person who has given 60-day notice to the Board — mandatory notice requirement
Companies: every person in charge of the company is deemed guilty unless they prove they had no knowledge — reverse burden of proof
